stem: A client has aphasia after a stroke. Which communication approach by the nurse is most appropriate during routine care?

options.A: Use short adult-level sentences at a comfortable volume, allow extra response time, and offer writing, pictures, or gestures when helpful.
options.B: Speak more loudly and repeat each question rapidly, then ask the family to answer whenever the client does not respond promptly.
options.C: Direct most questions to the family because aphasia makes the client's own responses unreliable, using the client mainly for simple yes-or-no choices.
options.D: Use spoken language without writing or gestures during routine care so the client practices verbal expression each time communication is needed.

rationale: ASHA recommends simple but adult language, a comfortable voice level, slower speech, short sentences, adequate time for the person to communicate, and multimodal supports such as pictures, gestures, writing, drawing, or pointing when useful. ASHA also cautions against assumptions about a person's intelligence or capabilities, and its aphasia guidance notes that aphasia does not itself imply cognitive deficits. Therefore A is correct. B adds unnecessary loudness and speed and prematurely bypasses the client. C assumes unreliability or incapacity from aphasia alone. D removes compensatory communication methods that can improve functional communication during care.
educational_objective: Communicate with an adult who has post-stroke aphasia by using clear adult-level language, an appropriate pace and volume, adequate response time, and individualized multimodal supports without assuming cognitive incapacity.
source_document_title: Aphasia — ASHA Practice Portal; Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder
source_locator: ASHA Practice Portal > Aphasia > Differential Diagnosis: aphasia does not imply cognitive deficits. Partner Approaches > Conversational Coaching and Supported Conversation for Adults With Aphasia: communication partners may use drawing, gesturing, cueing, confirming, summarizing, and multimodal communication. ASHA Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder > To help someone understand you better: comfortable voice level, simple but adult words, slower speech, short sentences, pictures/gestures/writing; > To help someone express themselves better: give time to communicate and invite drawing, writing, pointing, or gesturing; > To help people better understand AND express themselves: do not make assumptions about intelligence or capabilities.
source_claim_supported: Effective communication with adults who have aphasia uses adult-level simplified language, appropriate pace and volume, extra response time, and multimodal supports, while avoiding assumptions that aphasia implies cognitive incapacity.

supporting_sources.document_title: Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder
supporting_sources.locator: Sections 'To help someone understand you better,' 'To help someone express themselves better,' and 'To help people better understand AND express themselves.'
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Use comfortable volume, simple adult language, slower short sentences, response time, and multimodal strategies such as pictures, writing, pointing, and gestures; avoid assumptions about capability.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, printed pp. 30 and 33: use therapeutic communication techniques; recognize nonverbal cues. Therapeutic Communication, printed p. 33: assess verbal and nonverbal communication needs; allow time to communicate with the client; use therapeutic communication techniques; evaluate effectiveness of communication.
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication adapted to post-stroke aphasia
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four responses to remove the absolute-word distractor cue and make the alternatives realistic communication errors involving pace/volume, family substitution, and withholding compensatory modalities. The corrected item preserves the aphasia-communication construct with current ASHA guidance and a direct NCSBN Therapeutic Communication locator.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — concise neurologic communication scenario focused on routine nursing interaction rather than speech-language therapy technique.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects ASHA-supported adult language, pace/volume, response time, and multimodal communication; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — repetition and family support can have roles, but loud/rapid speech and premature substitution of family responses undermine effective client communication.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — family involvement can support care, but aphasia alone does not justify assuming the client's responses are unreliable or bypassing direct participation.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — spoken-language practice can occur in therapy, but routine nursing communication should not withhold compensatory modalities that improve functional communication.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that consistently supports direct, adult, multimodal client communication without an added contradictory practice.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B uses inappropriate speed/volume and bypass; C assumes incapacity; D removes supported communication modalities.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are similar in length and specificity, and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Psychosocial Integrity explicitly includes allowing time to communicate, assessing communication needs, and using therapeutic communication techniques.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether family-mediated communication or speech-only practice could be equally defensible; current ASHA guidance prioritizes direct client participation and multimodal supports and explicitly rejects assumptions about capability, leaving A uniquely best.
